volumetric: Unusual amount of data or events over a defined observation window.
Directional flow counters, exports, object access or audit events; record whether units are bytes, objects, rows or events.
Compare aligned windows within a workload/role. Evaluate empirical quantiles or an appropriate location/scale model.
Backups, reporting, synchronization and incident recovery can create large legitimate volumes.
frequency-rate: Unusual event frequency per entity and unit of observed time.
Authentication, API, process or DNS events, with collection completeness and event deduplication.
Measure count, duration, source diversity and target breadth. Check dispersion and seasonality before choosing a Poisson model.
Retries, outages, load tests and shared gateways can resemble an attack burst.
temporal: Activity inconsistent with a defined time-of-day, shift or seasonal context.
Event-time identity, administration and workload logs plus time-zone and schedule context.
Compare like calendar periods; handle travel, daylight-saving changes and ingestion delay.
On-call work, international teams and scheduled maintenance are legitimate alternatives.
peer-group: An entity differs from an explicitly defined comparison cohort.
Identity and asset inventory, role history, application use and access records.
Validate cohort membership, then compare distributions or fit a clustering model. TF-IDF can weight input features; it is not clustering itself.
Role changes, small cohorts and incomplete personnel data can create misleading outliers.
sequence: An event sequence differs from an expected operational workflow.
Process ancestry, authentication, application actions, session identifiers and event time.
Use explicit sequence constraints or a validated sequence model; define allowed lateness and missing steps.
Different legitimate workflows and timestamp disorder can produce the same apparent sequence.
graph-relationship: A new or unusual edge, path or community relationship.
Verified identities, effective permissions, resource ownership, authentication and network observations.
Define graph direction, edge meaning, observation window and novelty against a past-only graph.
Migrations, new projects and automated infrastructure can legitimately create many edges.
geographic-asn: A change in the network/location context associated with an identity.
Sign-in/VPN records, device context and versioned IP/ASN/geolocation enrichment.
Compare the account and device history; treat geolocation as uncertain and account for VPN/proxy egress.
Mobile networks, privacy relays, travel and shared egress can create apparent impossible travel.
identity-access: An unexpected authentication property, permission or identity relationship.
IdP, factor lifecycle, consent, token-validation and workload audit data where available.
Separate observed state changes, provider risk detections and inferred anomaly features.
Recovery, legitimate consent, role changes and delegated administration require investigation context.
rare-process-service: Low observed prevalence of a process or service in a stated population.
Process/service creation, software inventory, signer/hash and collection coverage.
Measure prevalence within a role and time period; distinguish new telemetry from a genuinely new binary.
Deployment, troubleshooting and rare authorized tools can all be legitimate.
parent-child: An unusual direct process relationship or explicitly defined ancestry path.
Stable process identifiers, parent identifiers, command lines, user and asset role.
Specify direct child versus ancestor matching and test process-ID reuse and incomplete ancestry.
Application automation can launch shells; in-process activity can evade child-process rules.
data-movement: Unexpected access, export, copy or synchronization involving a source and destination.
Application/storage audit, destination account, object sensitivity and transfer counters where available.
Keep event counts, distinct objects, bytes and records separate; evaluate destination and authorization context.
Approved export, backup, migration and collaboration can resemble exfiltration.
protocol-application: Unusual use of a protocol, application function or destination for an entity.
Protocol-aware sensors, endpoint attribution and application audit, with parser/version details.
Define the feature explicitly: record types, endpoint usage, negotiated attributes or destination novelty.
New clients, protocol changes and legitimate encoded identifiers can invalidate a historical baseline.
negative-absence: An expected observation is absent during a period where it should be observable.
Independent collector health, source heartbeat, delivery status, asset state and expected workload.
Model expected presence and detection delay separately from actual zero activity.
Outage, retirement, filtering, permissions and retention are alternatives to deliberate impairment.
state-change: A change to configuration, trust, permissions or exposure that warrants contextual review.
Before/after state, actor, control-plane audit, object identity and approved change records.
Scope the object and policy; first occurrence is a feature, not a maliciousness verdict.
Administrative changes can be legitimate, including changes to sensitive objects.
multi-event-correlation: A composition method joining related evidence, not a fifteenth independent statistical family.
Cross-source events with reliable tenant, identity, asset, session and time keys.
Specify equality keys and temporal constraints; measure the recall cost of each added gate.
Unrelated events, duplicate observations and correlated models can inflate confidence without adding independent evidence.
